content: Pecan Springs Elementary School needs a web-based learning game that helps sixth-grade students improve their fraction-solving skills. Students should answer fraction questions as part of an interactive game and receive feedback based on their performance. The project should also provide a common web menu through which students and teachers can access Space Fractions alongside related educational games.

The biggest improvement we want is for students to become more accurate and confident with fraction operations, especially adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing fractions. That matters most during independent practice, intervention groups, and any time a student is working through math centers or homework support, because those are the moments when they need extra repetition and immediate feedback.

We’d want the game to use standard fraction notation, like 1/2 or 3/4, and the same terms students hear in class, such as numerator, denominator, equivalent fractions, and simplest form. It should accept answers as reduced fractions, mixed numbers when appropriate, and whole numbers if that’s the correct result. If possible, it should also show models like number lines or visual fraction bars, because that matches how we teach them.

It should stay around a sixth-grade reading level, but with very short sentences and familiar classroom wording. We’d want it to avoid fancy vocabulary and use direct prompts like “Solve,” “Choose,” or “Try again,” so students who need support can follow along without getting stuck on the wording. If there’s any new term, it should be explained right away in simple language.

It should save records by student name and class group so teachers can see progress for each class and each student. We’d want it tied to the student’s classroom roster if possible, rather than relying on free typing, so names stay consistent and easy to sort. If there’s a way to let teachers choose or manage the class group at login, that would be best.

Yes, if full names aren’t appropriate, the game should be able to use initials or some anonymous student ID instead. That would mainly apply when records are being displayed to other students or in any public-facing area, but teachers should still be able to match the record back to the right student in their own view.

We need it to work on the Chromebooks the students already use, and ideally also on regular desktop and laptop computers in the school. Chrome is the main browser we rely on, so that’s the most important one to support, and it would be nice if it also works in Edge or Firefox if the school happens to use them. I’m not aware of any special restrictions beyond the usual school filtering and managed devices, but we’d want to avoid anything that depends on installing software or allowing pop-ups.

It should handle slow or spotty connections as gracefully as possible, because that happens in the school building sometimes. I’d still expect it to need internet to start up and save records, but if the connection drops briefly during a session, it shouldn’t lose the student’s work right away. If it has to pause or reconnect, that’s fine, as long as it makes the situation clear and doesn’t wipe out progress.

It should give immediate, encouraging feedback that the answer was incorrect without sounding harsh. Then it should give the student another chance, maybe with a hint or a simpler reminder of the steps, instead of just moving on. If they keep missing it, the game can still show the correct answer and let them continue so they don’t get stuck too long.

For the first version, I’d consider it successful if students can log in, play fraction questions in a game format, get clear feedback, and teachers can see basic progress by student and class. It also needs to fit into the school’s existing web menu and work reliably on the school devices. The main open questions for me are the exact scoring or progress rules, how detailed the teacher reports should be, and whether the login should use full names, initials, or an ID by default.

I’d want the menu grouped by subject or grade level first, then the games listed underneath in a simple, consistent order. Space Fractions should probably appear with the other sixth-grade math activities, and if there are favorites or most-used games, those could be pinned near the top for convenience. The main goal is that a student can find it quickly without having to search through a long list.

It should work both ways. Most of the time I’d expect students to use it independently during practice time, but teachers should be able to guide a whole class lesson, a small group, or a review session when they want to. That might change if a teacher is introducing a new fraction skill, supporting struggling students, or using it as a quick assessment, because then they may want more control over what students see and when they move on.

Ideally the teacher would introduce it with the class, make sure everyone can get in, and then let students work through it while helping anyone who gets stuck. In that first rollout, the teacher would probably spend more time monitoring and answering questions than actively directing every step. A different approach might be needed if the class is very new to the devices, if the teacher wants to use it as a guided lesson, or if there are students who need extra support or more challenge.

Yes, it should handle those differences reasonably well. It needs to work on the school’s standard browsers and on both tablets and laptops, because we use both, and if a browser isn’t supported it should tell the user clearly instead of failing silently. Home access would be nice if allowed, but school use is the priority, and I’d want it to behave the same way whether the student is on campus or at home as long as their account can get in.

Yes, we’d want it to stay tightly school-appropriate. The content should stick to fractions and the space theme, with no outside links, no ads, no chat, and only age-appropriate images and language. I would also expect any new content or major update to be reviewed by school staff before students see it, at least for the first release and probably for future changes too.

For the default, I’d want it tied to the student’s school login so teachers can match records without confusion. In most cases the display could use the student’s first name or full name depending on what the school prefers, but I’d avoid using a school ID as the primary thing students see. We might switch to initials only if privacy concerns come up in shared spaces or reports that students can see.

It should feel like a smooth handoff rather than starting over. Ideally they can click from Space Fractions back to the common menu and choose the next game from the same place, with the teacher able to direct them if needed. In normal classroom use, I’d want that transition to be quick and simple so students don’t lose time or get confused.

I’d want them to choose it from a list in the common menu. That gives teachers and students a clear starting point and makes it easier to switch between games without any confusion. If the teacher is guiding the class, they could still direct everyone to click the same game at the same time.

Their progress in the first game should be saved automatically so they can come back to it later. If they leave in the middle of a round, I’d expect the game to remember where they were, or at least preserve their score and completion status. We wouldn’t want students losing work just because they switched to another activity.

It should mostly depend on how many times they’ve already tried that question and maybe how far along they are in the lesson. I’d want the game to give a hint first, then a simpler reminder if they miss it again, and only after that show the correct answer so they can keep moving. The point is to help them learn without getting stuck too long on one problem.

I’d expect it to cover the main sixth-grade fraction skills, especially adding and subtracting fractions, comparing fractions, and maybe simplifying or finding equivalent fractions. If the team thinks it fits the curriculum, multiplying and dividing fractions could be included too, but I’d want the basics to come first. The exact mix should match what the teachers are trying to reinforce.

It should use the same classroom language the students already know, so terms like numerator, denominator, equivalent fractions, and simplest form should be used consistently. For visuals, fraction bars and number lines would be the most useful, and the game should pick whichever one makes the problem easiest to understand. If the fraction is improper or the answer is greater than one, the visual may need to show a whole plus a part or extend past one on the number line so it still makes sense.

I’d want it to follow a planned progression rather than feel random. It should start with the skill the teacher assigned or the lesson is focused on, then move to the next related skill once the student shows they’re ready. If the system can also repeat a topic when a student is struggling, that would be helpful too.

It should still start with the teacher’s assigned skill by default, because that keeps the whole class on the same learning target. If the game can tell the student is doing very well, it could offer harder questions after a few correct answers, but I wouldn’t want it skipping ahead immediately on its own. Teachers should stay in control of the main path.

I’d think “ready” means they’ve answered several questions correctly in a row with little or no help, not just one lucky guess. If they’re getting hints a lot or missing the same type of problem, they should keep practicing the current skill. I don’t know the exact number of correct answers we’d use, but it should be based on consistent performance, not a single score.

If a student is missing multiple questions in the same skill, using hints every time, or taking more than one attempt on most problems, that should count as struggling. I’d also treat repeated mistakes on the same concept as a sign they need more practice before moving ahead. The game should slow down there rather than push them into harder work too soon.

It should keep them on the same skill and give more practice first, with additional hints or a simpler version of the problem if needed. I wouldn’t want to cap retries too hard, because the point is learning, but after a few misses it should switch to more guidance instead of just repeating the same thing. If the student still isn’t getting it, the teacher should be able to see that and step in.

After a few misses on the same type of problem, it should start giving a simpler version or more explicit hints rather than just another identical question. If the student is still stuck after that, the game should flag it for the teacher pretty quickly, ideally within the same session so the teacher can help while the lesson is still fresh. I’d want the teacher to see that the student needs support, but I don’t know that we need a very exact number of attempts unless the team wants one.

It should preserve the student’s current place in the skill path, their current score or progress in that session, and whether they were in the middle of a question. I’d keep the stored details limited to school use, so students and teachers can see progress, but we shouldn’t expose personal data or more score detail than is needed for learning. If there are privacy rules from the district, we’d want to follow those closely.

I don’t know the exact district policy off the top of my head, so we’d need to verify that with the school or district. My expectation is that progress, answers, and time spent are probably fine if they’re used for instruction, but teacher notes and anything personally sensitive should be handled carefully and only stored if there’s a clear need. If there are fields the district considers off-limits, we should not retain those at all.

We should follow whatever the district says for educational records and student privacy, and if they don’t give a tighter rule, I’d keep only what’s needed for instruction and teacher review. That would usually mean retaining progress, answers, and time spent for a reasonable period, but avoiding anything unnecessary like freeform personal comments, sensitive identifiers, or notes unrelated to the game. Anything the district classifies as restricted should either be excluded entirely or stored in a more limited way with access only for authorized staff.

Anything that affects student privacy, prevents students from completing the learning flow, or gives teachers unreliable progress information should be treated as major. If those come up, I’d want them fixed before rollout rather than worked around, because those are core to whether the game is usable in the classroom. Smaller issues like cosmetic bugs can wait, but anything that breaks learning or reporting needs to be escalated right away.

If student data is visible to the wrong user, if a child can get into another child’s progress, or if the game stores information it should not be storing, that’s an immediate blocker. Also, if teachers can’t trust the scores or a session can’t be resumed safely, I’d treat that as serious enough to escalate before launch. Anything that could put the school at risk with privacy compliance or disrupt a live classroom session should not wait until after release.

If the issue exposes any student identity, session data, or teacher notes to unauthorized people, that should stop release immediately. I’d also stop release if the game can’t reliably separate one student’s data from another’s, or if there’s a risk of a student being directed into the wrong content in a way that could disrupt class. Basically, anything that creates a real privacy violation or a classroom safety concern needs to be treated as a release blocker, not a later fix.

Any new content should stay age-appropriate for sixth graders, support the learning goal, and not distract from fractions. Space science elements and characters are fine if they’re clearly part of the game theme, but they shouldn’t introduce anything scary, violent, or off-topic. Links to other activities should stay within the school-approved menu and related educational games, and anything added later should still fit the district’s standards for classroom use.

Adding new fraction problems and new practice modes should be allowed as long as they still reinforce the same math skills and are appropriate for sixth graders. Changing the story theme is okay too, but only if it stays lightweight and doesn’t pull attention away from the fraction work. I would disallow updates that shift the game into a different subject, become too complex for the grade level, or add mechanics that make it harder for students to practice fractions clearly.

If a student can understand what to do with a quick explanation and start playing without a lot of extra instructions, that’s probably still simple enough. Once a mode needs multiple steps, lots of branching rules, or more reading than the math itself, it’s getting too complicated. I’d also watch for whether the teacher would need to spend extra time explaining it in class, because if so, it’s probably beyond what we want for this project.

I’d want proper fraction symbols and standard math terms to be used, because the students should get comfortable with the real notation they’ll see in class. That said, simplified wording and visuals are fine if they help explain the concept without changing the math meaning. I would avoid slang or overly casual labels, and I’d want the terminology to stay consistent across the game and teacher-facing parts.
